---
title: "Energy participation and loss"
description: "What energy participation ratios mean, how they are normalized, and how they relate to loss."
scgsim-kind: "concept"
scgsim-status: "CONVERGING"
scgsim-id: "docs/eigenmode-epr"
---

A resonant mode stores energy in its fields and in circuit elements such as
a junction. The **energy participation ratio** (EPR) of a part of the model is
the fraction of the mode's energy stored there. Combined with that part's loss
tangent, it tells you how much that part contributes to the mode's loss.

The [energy-participation method of Minev et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.00620)
uses modes of a linearized Josephson circuit as inputs to quantization.
SCGSim computes the participation ratios and the loss they imply. It does not
build the nonlinear Hamiltonian, Kerr coefficients or qubit lifetime from
them.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  F["Mode fields"] --> P["Energy partitions"]
  P --> V["Bulk / surface / junction"]
  V --> L["Known-loss contributions"]
  A["Material loss assumptions"] --> L
```

## Three views of a mode {#workflow-and-state-contract}

| View | Energy attributed to | Physical question |
|---|---|---|
| Bulk | A modeled dielectric volume | How much electric energy lies in this material? |
| Surface | A thin-film interface estimate | How strongly does the field sample this interface? |
| Junction/port | A declared linearized circuit element | How does this element participate in the mode? |

A surface estimate takes the field at an interface and estimates the energy
in a thin film of given thickness and permittivity there. Metal–air (MA),
metal–substrate (MS) and substrate–air (SA) are different interfaces. Bulk and
surface values overlap: they are not separate pieces of one energy budget.
The junction is the linearized element you declared, with its inductance and
optional capacitance.

## Quantities and normalization {#quantities-and-normalization}

For an energy numerator $U_i$, participation is dimensionless:

$$
p_i = \frac{U_i}{U_{\mathrm{norm}}}.
$$

The denominator differs between solvers. AEDT uses the electric energy of all
physical domains plus the junction's capacitive energy. Palace uses its own
electric-domain and capacitive-energy tables. Thin-film energies are only
numerators; they are not added to the denominator.
The [surface and junction formulas](specs/aedt-runtime.qmd#surface-estimates-and-junction-normalization)
define the field convention and each supported quantity.

Junction participation is also defined differently. Palace reports a signed
port participation whose sign depends on the mode's phase convention. AEDT
reports nonnegative inductive ($p_L$) and capacitive ($p_C$) energy ratios.
Do not compare them as the same number.

The outer boundary matters too. Palace Eigenmode without an assigned
boundary uses PMC; HFSS uses Perfect E on the outer surfaces of its region
([HFSS 2024 R2 guide](https://ansyshelp.ansys.com/public/Views/Secured/Electronics/v242/en/PDFs/An%20Introduction%20to%20HFSS.pdf)).
Record the boundary and vacuum size with every result.

## Interfaces and loss assumptions {#surface-identity-masks-and-loss-assumptions}

For a dielectric channel with a known loss tangent, the modeled contribution is

$$
Q_i^{-1} = p_i\tan\delta_i.
$$

Both factors matter: a material the field barely touches can still dominate
if its loss tangent is large. Film thickness, permittivity and loss tangent are
your assumptions; the layout does not determine them. Summing over the
evaluated channels gives the loss from those channels only. It is not the
device's total $Q$ or $T_1$.

A loss tangent set to zero means lossless. A loss tangent you did not set is
unknown, and its contribution is left out of the sum. Likewise, energy that was
not computed is not zero energy.

::: {.callout-note title="Reading older Palace results" collapse="true"}
For Palace surface-film records preceding v2, a recorded zero loss tangent has
ambiguous origin. The reader preserves the raw value but treats its effective
loss as unknown; the inverse-$Q$ contribution remains unavailable.
:::

A **mask margin** is passed to Palace's native Inset evaluation as
`Mask: {Type: Inset, Margin: ...}`. Use a Palace build that supports this
evaluation. These results are separate from the retired SGB geometric distance
bands. Read the unmasked baseline and each returned margin separately; do not
add them. AEDT evaluates only horizontal (top and bottom) interfaces, not
sidewalls. Palace sidewalls are computed only where selected. You can change
loss tangents on a stored result without solving again; see
[Change loss assumptions offline](course/offline-epr.qmd).

The solver's own $Q$ and this $p\tan\delta$ sum are different quantities. The
solver $Q$ includes only the losses in the solver's model, such as lossy
materials or ports. Palace reports $Q = +\infty$ when the model has no loss;
that does not mean the device is lossless. See the
[native Q reference](specs/palace-eigenmode.qmd#native-eigenmode-q).

## Explore a result

Start with the [resonance tutorial](tutorials/resonance-epr/prepare.qmd), then use
[Change loss assumptions offline](course/offline-epr.qmd) to try other loss
values.

For binding and API details, use the [AEDT EPR reference](specs/aedt-runtime.qmd#public-epr-candidate-surface)
and [Palace Eigenmode reference](specs/palace-eigenmode.qmd). The
[report reference](report-model.qmd#eigenmode-epr-presentation) describes
selections, ordering and the separation of baseline, margin and unavailable
quantities.
